title: Cosine similarity and why we normalize
summary: Ranking by dot product means a document concatenated to itself beats an exact match. Cosine fixes that by comparing direction and discarding magnitude, and normalizing at index time makes it cost a single multiply-accumulate.
html:
Day 4 gave you weighted vectors. Today you compare two of them, and the obvious way to do it is broken in a way that is worth seeing clearly, because the fix is the reason every vector database on earth stores its vectors the way it does.

The obvious thing, and why it fails

Two vectors, multiply matching dimensions, add up the results. The dot product:

dot(a, b) = sum over i of  a[i] * b[i]

Shared terms contribute, terms present in only one contribute zero. Reasonable. Now watch it break.

Work in two dimensions so you can check every number. Say a = [3, 4] is your query and b = [6, 8] is a document. Notice b is exactly 2a: same direction, twice the magnitude. In text terms, b is the same document with every sentence written twice.

dot(a, a) = 3*3 + 4*4 = 25
dot(a, b) = 3*6 + 4*8 = 50

Rank by dot product and the duplicated document scores twice as high as an exact match against the query itself. Concatenate a document to itself and you have doubled its score without adding one new fact. Any ranking function with that property is not a ranking function, it is an exploit waiting to be found. Early web spam worked precisely like this.

Euclidean distance has the mirror problem. It reports a and b as far apart because one is longer, even though they are about exactly the same thing in exactly the same proportions.

Direction is the signal, magnitude is the noise

Here is the reframe that fixes it. In a term vector, direction encodes what the document is about, the mix of topics. Magnitude encodes how much text there is.

You want the first and not the second. A three sentence answer and a three page answer on the same subject should be equally retrievable. So throw magnitude away and compare direction only. That is the cosine of the angle between the vectors:

cos(a, b) = dot(a, b) / ( |a| * |b| )

where |a| = sqrt( sum over i of a[i]^2 )      the L2 norm

Run the same numbers. |a| = sqrt(9+16) = 5 and |b| = sqrt(36+64) = 10.

cos(a, b) = 50 / (5 * 10) = 1.000    identical direction, as it should be
cos(a, a) = 25 / (5 * 5)  = 1.000    and now these agree

The duplication exploit is gone. Add a third vector c = [4, 3], same length as a but a different topic mix:

cos(a, c) = (3*4 + 4*3) / (5 * 5) = 24 / 25 = 0.960

Close but not identical, which is right. Same terms, different emphasis.

The trick that makes it free

Look at where the cost sits. Every comparison needs two square roots and a division, and you pay them on every query against every candidate. At a million candidates that is a million divisions you did not need to do.

But |a| does not depend on the query. It is a property of the document, known at index time. So divide each vector by its own norm once, when you write it:

a_hat = a / |a| = [3/5, 4/5] = [0.6, 0.8]
b_hat = b / |b| = [6/10, 8/10] = [0.6, 0.8]      same vector now

dot(a_hat, b_hat) = 0.6*0.6 + 0.8*0.8 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.000

Once every stored vector has unit length, cosine similarity is just the dot product. No square roots, no division, one multiply-accumulate per dimension, which is the operation CPUs and GPUs are best at. On modern hardware it is a single fused instruction per element.

This is ordinary systems thinking: move invariant work out of the hot path and precompute it into the stored representation. It is the same instinct as denormalising a column you always filter on. It is also why, when you read a vector database's internals later in this course, you will find that "cosine" and "inner product" are frequently the same code path with a normalisation flag set at ingest.

Two things people get wrong

Cosine scores are not calibrated. A score of 0.82 does not mean 82 percent relevant. It does not mean anything on its own. The number depends on your corpus, your weighting scheme, and your vocabulary size, and it shifts when any of those change. Cosine is useful for ordering candidates, and that is all. Teams that hardcode a threshold like "return everything above 0.75" discover this when they swap embedding models and the threshold silently becomes meaningless. If you need a cutoff, calibrate it against a labelled set (Day 57) rather than picking a round number that looks confident.

Cosine is not always the right metric. For TF-IDF it plainly is, because weights are non-negative and only direction carries meaning, which conveniently bounds the score to the range 0 to 1. For the neural embeddings you meet on Day 9, it depends on how the model was trained. Most are trained with a cosine objective and ship pre-normalised, so it does not matter. Some are trained with an unnormalised inner product, where magnitude carries real signal, and normalising throws information away. This is not settled doctrine you can assume: read the model card, and if it says to normalise, normalise. Getting this wrong costs a few points of recall and produces no error message, which is the worst kind of bug.

Where you are

You can now build vectors from text and rank them against a query. That is a complete retrieval system, and if you did the Day 4 exercise you are most of the way to having written one.

Which raises the question you have been able to postpone until now: what exactly is a document? You have been assuming chunks exist. Tomorrow is Chunking 101, where you decide how to cut text into the units you actually index, and find out how much that single decision constrains everything downstream.
exercise:
1. Reproduce the failure. Take your Day 4 TF-IDF code and add a dot(a, b) function. Score a short query against a document, then against that same document with its text concatenated to itself. Confirm the doubled version wins. Then add cosine and confirm the two now tie. Seeing your own scorer get this wrong once is worth more than reading about it.

2. Normalize at index time. Change your code to divide every document vector by its L2 norm when you build it, and change your scorer to a plain dot product. Verify the rankings are identical to the cosine version. That is the optimisation every vector store makes, now made by you.

3. Check the calibration claim. Run your scorer over the same query on two different corpora, one small and one several times larger. Compare the top score in each. It will differ, sometimes a lot, for the same query and the same best match. Write the two numbers down. That is the argument against hardcoded thresholds, in your own data.
